claims.text: Stability of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and the enthalpic drive for metal segregation.
Maintaining an equiatomic or near-equiatomic distribution provides high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution under high-temperature conditions.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation under high-temperature conditions.
A uniform distribution of metal atoms throughout the lattice maximizes configurational entropy.
A uniform atomic distribution protects the alloy from phase segregation.
A uniform atomic distribution protects the alloy from chemical decomposition.
The configurational-entropy contribution compensates for enthalpic forces that drive phase separation.
Even slight departures from equiatomic composition reduce the configurational-entropy contribution.
The entropy reduction caused by slight compositional deviations permits localized metal segregation and eventual destabilization of the solid solution at high temperature.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve a single-phase crystal structure throughout thermal cycling from 473 to 1923 K in a controlled inert atmosphere.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve a homogeneous chemical distribution throughout thermal cycling from 473 to 1923 K in a controlled inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticles deliberately deviated by approximately 10–15% from equiatomic composition will exhibit phase separation under the same thermal-cycling conditions.
Nanoparticles deliberately deviated by approximately 10–15% from equiatomic composition will develop chemical heterogeneity under the same thermal-cycling conditions.
An inert or controlled atmosphere inhibits oxidation sufficiently for the proposed entropy-versus-segregation mechanism to govern the comparison.
Extreme compositional deviations or oxidizing conditions may activate alternative degradation pathways.
The cited evidence set provides no direct evidence quantifying the configurational-entropy contribution to stability over 473–1923 K.
